entries.what_happened: Two manuscripts. (a) 'Primitive roots for every admissible integer base' claims that for every integer a that is neither -1 nor a square there are c_a > 0 and x_a >= 2 such that, for every real x >= x_a, at least c_a x/(log x)^2 primes p in (x, 2x) satisfy p not dividing a and ord_p(a) = p - 1 (the main theorem of the introduction; the abstract states the same). The proof (01a-reduction.tex) builds primes p = c r Q + 1 with c in {2, 4}, Q > x^0.9 prime, and every prime factor of r in (exp((log x)^0.1), exp((log x)^0.3)), inside a residue class modulo M = 8 times the odd primes dividing a, chosen so that (a/p) = -1. This makes the index (p-1)/ord_p(a) odd. Primes whose index has Q as a factor are discarded using a bound on the product of |a^j - 1| for j up to 2x^0.1. Primes whose index has a prime factor l dividing r are discarded using a uniform Kummer-splitting bound (stated in 01a-reduction.tex, proved in 07-splitting.tex), which rests on the Hecke zero-free theorem (Theorem 1.2). (b) 'Simultaneous primitive roots: a conditional lower bound for prime bases' proves that for any finite set of distinct positive primes q_1, ..., q_k there are at least c x/(log x)^2 primes p in (x, 2x) with p not dividing q_1...q_k and ord_p(q_i) = p - 1 for every i. It does this only under four stated Inputs (see conditional_on). Its k = 1 case is the Artin infinitude count restricted to positive prime bases.
entries.delivers: For (a), the claim proves the infinitude assertion for every admissible base, and the statement matches the list's. The list asks, for each integer a that is not a square and not -1, whether a is a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes. The lower bound in (a) is positive in every sufficiently large dyadic interval, which gives infinitude. Restrictions: c_a and x_a depend on a, which the text states, and no uniformity in a is claimed. Negative bases other than -1 (for example -2, -3, -4) are covered by the signed squarefree decomposition a = d0 t^2 in the progression lemma, with the row d0 = -1 handling negative squares, and the Kummer bound is stated for |a| > 1. For (b), the claim gives infinitude only for positive prime bases, one or several at a time, and only conditionally on the four Inputs. It adds no unconditional case beyond (a) and does not cover composite or negative bases.
entries.remains: If (a) is correct, the infinitude statement of the bullet is fully covered and nothing in it remains open. Not established by either manuscript: the predicted order x/log x (the manuscripts prove x/(log x)^2 only), the asymptotic density with Artin's constant mentioned in the Wikipedia lead (outside the bullet), and any uniformity of c_a and x_a in a. For (b), the unconditional simultaneous case remains open, and so do all bases that are not positive primes.
entries.direction: proves the infinitude assertion for every admissible base (a); conditional proof of infinitude for positive prime bases, simultaneously (b)
entries.conditional_on: (a) assumes no hypothesis of its own, but depends on work outside its text: (i) 'The Poisson-Dirichlet law for the prime factors of p-1', Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 5.2, for the one-sided marked Type II estimate; the text says its coefficient criterion (Lemma 10.2) extracts the coefficient dependence from that companion's argument. (ii) 'The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis', Part I, Sections 5-7, whose coefficient reflection and additive probe the text adapts over each cyclotomic field. (iii) Dunn and Radziwill, Section 5.1 and Appendix A, for theta comparison formulas. (iv) Kazhdan and Patterson's cubic theta representation with their erratum, and Patterson's cubic theta series, for the normalization. (v) The block-sieve and rough-density forms, adapted from 'BlockPaper' (Lemmas 2.9 and 7.4), with proofs included in the text. (b) assumes four Inputs, which it attributes to (a): the uniform Hecke zero-free assertion (the same as (a)'s Theorem 1.2: no zeros of L_F(s, eta) for Re s > 1 - 10^-6, for every finite-order Hecke character of a cyclotomic field containing mu_12); the marked Type II estimate in two parts, (i) the coefficient criterion (= (a)'s Lemma 10.2) and (ii) rough-factor cancellation (= (a)'s Proposition 10.3); the block sieve (= (a)'s Lemma 11.1); and the rough-number density (= (a)'s Lemma 11.2). Its splitting proof also takes the abelian tower argument and the prime-ideal count from (a)'s Section 9, equations (9.2) and (9.5)-(9.9), as cited.
entries.doubts: (a) The analytic core, Theorem 1.2, has no conductor or height cutoff and one width, 10^-6, for all cyclotomic fields containing mu_12 and all finite-order Hecke characters; the text says 'the width is common to all fields and characters in the statement'. The introduction describes the standard simultaneous zero-free regions as having logarithmic width and permitting at most one simple real exceptional zero (citing Thorner-Zaman, Theorem 3.1), and presents the common width as the new step. The text does not compare it with a published result of this strength. Cyclotomic Dedekind zeta functions factor into Dirichlet L-functions, so the statement as written also covers every Dirichlet L-function. The text does not discuss that consequence. The Hecke argument is described as built 'over each fixed F' from mechanisms of the companion 'The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis', which the introduction says treats Q(sqrt(-3)). The marked Type II estimate is imported from the Poisson-Dirichlet companion; the coefficient criterion's dependence is 'extracted' from that argument, and the introduction says the authors verify the character and frequency estimates themselves. (b) The four Inputs are hypotheses, and the text says their proofs lie in (a) and its companions, so (b) inherits the doubts in (a). The abstract's first sentence states the result without the condition, which appears only in its last sentence. The introduction counts four Inputs, but Input 2 has two parts, so there are five displayed hypotheses. Coverage: I did not read sections 02-06, the proof of Theorem 1.2, the fixed-progression construction in 12-construction.tex, or the appendix in full. A keyword search of those sections found no 'sketch' or 'left to the reader' style flags. The points above rest on the introduction, the reduction, the rough-Type II and sieve statements I read, and the Inputs of (b).
